claims.text: An integrated laser-melting drop-calorimetry, rapid-DSC, synchrotron X-ray, and CALPHAD workflow can accurately and efficiently characterize melting across a wide range of high-entropy alloys.
The integrated workflow can determine melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
Single-phase BCC high-entropy alloys suitable as initial samples can be produced by arc melting and homogenization.
Repeated arc melting improves chemical homogeneity in high-entropy-alloy ingots.
Additive manufacturing can produce well-mixed, single-phase BCC or FCC HEAs with minimal compositional segregation.
Real-time synchrotron X-ray measurements can capture phase evolution during the proposed laser-induced melting and rapid-cooling cycle.
The workflow can operate from room temperature to approximately 3000 °C for refractory HEAs.
A uniform single-phase BCC or FCC microstructure minimizes local segregation and defects.
Reduced segregation and defect content cause melting to occur more uniformly.
More uniform melting improves the reliability of latent-heat and volume-change measurements.
DSC heat-flow measurements quantify the thermal signal associated with melting.
Laser-drop calorimetry provides rapid, localized melting.
High-speed X-ray imaging can track expansion or contraction and thereby determine the volume or density change at melting.
CALPHAD-derived thermodynamic constraints can be combined with calorimetric and X-ray data to improve extraction of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, and density change.
The proposed measurements will have uncertainties of approximately ±5–10%.
Measured melting properties will show systematic composition-dependent trends aligned with CALPHAD predictions.
The approach is applicable primarily to compositionally homogeneous alloys whose melting points fall within the experimental temperature range.
Significant phase separation, high volatility, or non-equilibrium microstructures can place an alloy outside the effective range of the method.
Rapid convection in the molten state and minor microstructural inhomogeneities can degrade quantitative performance.
Consistent deviations greater than 15% from both CALPHAD predictions and standard DSC benchmarks, or uncontrolled sensitivity to slight inhomogeneity, would refute the proposed approach.
